resources.whatItTakes: Affiliate marketing is real work dressed up as passive income. You're building an audience — through a blog, YouTube channel, newsletter, or social account — and earning commissions when that audience buys through your links. The honest version: most of your early months are spent creating content that almost nobody sees yet. You need patience with delayed feedback loops, genuine curiosity about the products you promote, and enough consistency to keep publishing before the numbers justify it. SEO takes time. Trust takes longer. If you can write clearly, learn what your audience actually needs, and resist the urge to slap affiliate links on everything, you have a real shot.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most people fail at the content volume problem — they write four posts, see no traffic, and conclude it doesn't work. It's not that it didn't work; they stopped before the compounding started. The second failure mode is promoting too many unrelated products too early, which destroys audience trust before it's built. The third is chasing high-commission programs in saturated niches (VPNs, web hosting) instead of finding a narrower audience they actually understand and can serve honestly.
resources.theDip: Months two through five are brutal. You're publishing regularly, your analytics show mostly bots and your own visits, and you haven't made a dollar. This is the dip. It's not a sign you chose wrong — it's the standard experience. Affiliate income is backloaded: the content you write in month three often earns its first commission in month seven. The people who get through this period treat it like building infrastructure, not waiting for a lottery ticket. Set a 90-day commitment before you evaluate whether to continue.

aiPrompts.task: Niche scoring (broad affiliate — Amazon + SaaS + digital)

Score this niche for general affiliate marketing.

Niche: [your candidate]
Your background / interest: [why this niche]
Target audience: [demographic + buying behavior]

Output:

NICHE FIT (1-10):
- Audience size + buying intent
- Affiliate program density (how many programs you can stack)
- Commission ceiling (Amazon 1-10%, SaaS 25-50%, digital 30-50%)
- Trust threshold (some niches require deep credibility)
- Saturation (top sites already dominating SERP)

TOP 10 PROGRAMS to apply to in this niche (mix of types):
- Amazon Associates (default 1-10%)
- 3-5 SaaS programs with recurring commissions
- 2-3 digital product / course programs
- 1-2 high-ticket / coaching programs

CONTENT ENGINE (3 formats that win in this niche):
- Comparison content (Tool A vs B)
- Tutorial / how-to with affiliate mention
- Listicles (best X for Y)

DISTRIBUTION (1-2 channels to focus on):
- SEO blog (compounds long-term)
- YouTube (visual demos)
- Newsletter (highest conversion)

90-DAY EARNINGS PROJECTION:
- Month 1: 0-100
- Month 2-3: 100-500
- Month 4-6: 500-2K
- Month 12+: 2K-15K

Be honest if niche is overcrowded.

aiPrompts.task: Comparison post (Tool A vs Tool B — highest-converting affiliate format)
aiPrompts.prompt:
Write an honest comparison post: [Tool A] vs [Tool B] for [target use case].

My affiliate: [which one I'm an affiliate for — be transparent]
My honest verdict: [where each one wins]

Structure:

INTRO (180 words):
- Who this comparison is for
- TL;DR verdict (one-line — pick X if Y, pick Z if W)
- FTC disclosure (visible, not buried)

COMPARISON TABLE:
8-10 dimensions side-by-side (pricing, features, integrations, learning curve, support, mobile, etc).

DETAILED SECTIONS (5-7):
For each, who wins + why with specific examples.

USE CASE WALKTHROUGHS:
- Use case 1 (Tool A wins)
- Use case 2 (Tool B wins)
- Use case 3 (it depends)

VERDICT:
- Pick A if [criteria]
- Pick B if [criteria]
- Pick neither if [edge case]

CTA + AFFILIATE LINKS (clearly disclosed).

Tone: honest reviewer, not marketer. Mention real downsides of your affiliate. Trust > one-time conversion.

commonMistakes.mistake: No FTC disclosure (or buried in footer)
commonMistakes.why: FTC enforces disclosure rules. Hidden disclosures = fines + program termination. Plus it is the right thing to do.
commonMistakes.prevention: Visible disclosure on every affiliate piece. "I may earn a commission if you buy through links here. I only recommend tools I personally use."

commonMistakes.mistake: Promoting low-trust products for short-term gains
commonMistakes.why: A bad recommendation tanks audience trust. One sketchy course or scammy SaaS = unsubscribes + reputation loss.
commonMistakes.prevention: Use every product 30+ days before recommending. Your reputation is the asset.

commonMistakes.mistake: Single-program dependency
commonMistakes.why: Programs change commission rates, pause programs, or kick affiliates with no notice. Single-source = single point of failure.
commonMistakes.prevention: Diversify across 5-10 programs.

commonMistakes.mistake: No email list — relying on social only
commonMistakes.why: Email is the only owned channel.
commonMistakes.prevention: Email list from day 1. Lead magnet → 7-day welcome → ongoing newsletter.

commonMistakes.mistake: Going broad ("personal finance tips") vs niche
commonMistakes.why: Broad audiences have low buying intent. Niche audiences trust your specific expertise.
commonMistakes.prevention: Pick a specific persona × specific outcome. "Side-income personal finance for educators" beats "personal finance tips."

commonMistakes.mistake: No SEO foundation — relying on social
commonMistakes.why: Social posts decay fast. SEO content compounds for years. Affiliates with 100+ ranking blog posts earn passively for years.
commonMistakes.prevention: 1-2 SEO posts per week minimum. Long-tail keywords. 12-month compounding view.

commonMistakes.mistake: Paid ads before knowing LTV
commonMistakes.why: Ads at break-even CAC require knowing customer lifetime value. Without 3-6 months of data, ad spend is gambling.
commonMistakes.prevention: No paid ads before 6 months of organic data. Once LTV is known, paid scales.

resources.whatItTakes: You're running social media accounts for small businesses — restaurants, gyms, boutiques, local service providers — and using AI tools to do the content creation and scheduling work faster than a traditional social media manager could. The actual job is understanding what a business owner wants their brand to feel like, translating that into a consistent posting rhythm, and reporting results in plain English. AI handles the drafting and image prompting; you handle the judgment, the client relationship, and the strategy. You need to be comfortable talking to business owners, learning new tools quickly, and staying calm when a client says 'this doesn't sound like us.' This is a service business, not a software product. Your income depends on keeping clients happy long enough to retain them month after month.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most people who quit do so in the first 60 days — before they have a single paying client — because the outreach feels embarrassing and the rejection is demoralizing. They send five or six messages, hear nothing back, and decide the market is too competitive. The second failure point is underpricing to get the first yes, then resenting the client and doing mediocre work. The third failure is over-relying on AI output without editing it. Clients notice when captions sound generic. One bad comment about 'robot content' can end a retainer.
resources.theDip: Month two and three are the hardest. You probably have one or two clients, the work is still taking longer than it should because you're building your systems, and you're not making enough to feel like this is real. The clients you have are asking for small changes constantly, and every revision feels like it's eating your margin. This is where most people either quietly stop responding to new leads or start taking on any client at any price just to feel momentum. The dip is real and it's specifically about patience before your process is fast enough to make the math work. Push through by timing yourself, building reusable templates, and not adding a third client until the first two are running smoothly.

You are a social media strategist helping me manage content for a client. Here are the details:

Business name: [CLIENT NAME]

aiPrompts.task: Write a client onboarding questionnaire and welcome email
aiPrompts.prompt:
I run an AI-assisted social media management service. I just signed a new client and need two things:

1. A client onboarding questionnaire (Google Form-style, 12-15 questions) that covers:
- Business basics (name, website, location)
- Target customer description
- Brand voice and personality (ask them to pick adjectives)
- Competitors they admire
- Content topics they want to own
- Topics or imagery to avoid
- Login access instructions
- Their definition of success for social media
- Preferred communication method and response time expectations

2. A warm, professional welcome email to send immediately after signing. The email should:
- Confirm what they've purchased and what happens next
- Set realistic expectations (results take 60-90 days to compound)
- Explain the onboarding process step by step
- Give them a direct point of contact and response time SLA
- End with genuine excitement without being over-the-top

Tone: warm, confident, and organized. This client is paying $[MONTHLY RETAINER] per month.

I manage social media for a business client and need to write their monthly performance report. Here is the raw data from the past 30 days:

Platform: [PLATFORM]

Follower count end: [NUMBER]

Average engagement rate: [%]

aiPrompts.task: Create a cold outreach message to land new clients
aiPrompts.prompt:
I offer AI-assisted social media management for small businesses. I want to reach out to potential clients who are clearly underusing social media. Help me write outreach messages for the following scenario:

Target business type: [e.g., local restaurant / boutique fitness studio / real estate agent / e-commerce brand]
Where I'm reaching out: [LinkedIn DM / cold email / Instagram DM]
What I noticed about their account: [e.g., they post once a month, their last post was 6 weeks ago, their captions are just product descriptions with no engagement]
What I offer: Done-for-you social media management starting at $[YOUR PRICE]/month. I use AI tools to keep costs low and turnaround fast.

Write 3 versions of the outreach message:
1. Short and direct (under 60 words)
2. Value-first with a specific observation (under 120 words)
3. Question-opener that invites a reply (under 80 words)

Do NOT use phrases like 'I hope this finds you well,' 'synergy,' 'game-changer,' or 'crush your goals.' Sound like a real person who noticed something specific about their business.

commonMistakes.mistake: Underpricing to get the first client and never recovering
commonMistakes.why: That client refers others at the same price, you fill your hours at unprofitable rates, and raising prices on existing clients is awkward and often causes churn. You end up working 20+ hours/week for less than minimum wage once you account for unpaid admin time.
commonMistakes.prevention: Price based on the value to their business, not your hours.

commonMistakes.mistake: Publishing AI-generated content without editing it for the client's real voice
commonMistakes.why: AI content is recognizably generic. Audiences disengage, the client notices their posts don't sound like them, and you get fired. Worse, some AI outputs repeat phrases like 'in today's fast-paced world' or 'dive in' that immediately signal automation to savvy readers.
commonMistakes.prevention: Treat AI output as a first draft, not a final product. Spend 10-15 minutes per content batch adding specific details (real customer names, actual product names, local references). Keep a 'voice notes' doc per client with their real phrases, jokes, and no-go words from the onboarding questionnaire.

commonMistakes.mistake: Managing client access through your own personal accounts
commonMistakes.why: Logging into client Instagram or Facebook through your personal device ties their account to your login history. If Meta flags unusual activity, BOTH your account and theirs can get locked. If the relationship ends badly, there's no clean handoff.
commonMistakes.prevention: Use a social media management tool (Buffer, Metricool, Later) that connects via official API. Never ask for client passwords directly — use platform-native team access features (Meta Business Suite, LinkedIn Page Admin, etc.) so clients can revoke access cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking on too many clients before building repeatable systems
commonMistakes.why: Month one with 3 clients feels manageable. Month two with 6 clients and no templates, no scheduling tool, and no reporting system means you're rebuilding everything from scratch for each client every week. Quality drops, deadlines slip, clients notice.
commonMistakes.prevention: Before client 3, build: a content calendar template, a monthly report template, a client folder structure, and a scheduling workflow in one tool. Cap yourself at 5 clients until your systems can run a client in under 3 hours/week.

commonMistakes.mistake: Promising follower growth or viral results in writing
commonMistakes.why: Social media results depend on platform algorithms, ad budgets, industry, and timing — none of which you fully control. If you write 'I'll grow your account by 500 followers in 30 days' in a contract or DM and don't deliver, you've created a legal and reputation problem.
commonMistakes.prevention: Promise deliverables you control: posts published, reports delivered, response time, content quality. Frame outcomes as possibilities with honest timelines ('most clients see meaningful engagement growth within 60-90 days'). Put this language explicitly in your contract.

decisionTrees.question: Should I specialize in a specific industry or stay a generalist?

options.choice: Pick one industry niche (e.g., restaurants, real estate agents, fitness studios)
options.pickIf: You have prior experience in that industry OR you've already landed your first client in that space and want to clone that success. Niching makes referrals faster and content creation easier because you reuse research.
options.nextStep: Build a niche-specific case study from your first client, update your outreach to speak directly to that industry's pain points, and list yourself in niche directories or Facebook groups for that industry.

options.pickIf: You're in the first 90 days with fewer than 3 clients and don't yet know which industry is most profitable or enjoyable for you. Generalism lets you test before committing.
options.nextStep: Track which client types take the least time, pay the most, and refer the most. After 3-4 clients, you'll have a clear answer about where to specialize.

decisionTrees.question: A client wants to add a platform (e.g., TikTok) that wasn't in the original scope. What do I do?

options.choice: Add it as a paid scope expansion
options.pickIf: The new platform requires meaningfully different content (especially video) or more than 2 additional hours per week. TikTok and YouTube Shorts are fundamentally different workflows from static post platforms.
options.nextStep: Get written approval before starting. Update the contract.

options.choice: Include it at no charge if it's truly minimal work
options.pickIf: The platform uses the same content format (e.g., adding Facebook when you already do Instagram, and you're just cross-posting). Only do this if it takes under 30 minutes/week and you want to build goodwill with a long-term client.
options.nextStep: Set a clear expectation in writing: 'I'll cross-post to Facebook at no charge — note this is repurposed content, not platform-native content.' This prevents the client from later expecting full platform management for free.

options.pickIf: You don't have the skills for that platform yet (e.g., video editing for TikTok) or you're already at capacity. Saying no is better than delivering bad work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking on clients in niches you don't understand
commonMistakes.why: AI content tools produce plausible-sounding text in any niche, but plausible isn't accurate. Medical, legal, financial, and highly technical niches require factual accuracy that AI alone can't guarantee. Clients in these spaces will catch errors, lose trust, and churn fast — sometimes after threatening legal action for published misinformation.
commonMistakes.prevention: Pick 1-2 niches you already have knowledge in or can research deeply. Build your first 3 case studies in those niches only. Expand to new verticals only after you have a human subject-matter expert (SME) review process in place.

commonMistakes.mistake: Promising ranking results on a fixed timeline
commonMistakes.why: SEO timelines depend on domain authority, competition level, Google's crawl schedule, and algorithm updates — none of which you control. Operators who promise 'page 1 in 90 days' either get lucky or face angry clients and chargebacks when it doesn't happen.
commonMistakes.prevention: Promise inputs, not outputs. Contracts should specify deliverables (articles published, audits completed, backlinks built) not ranking positions. Set expectations in the sales call: 'Most clients see measurable traffic movement in 3-6 months. Rankings take longer. Here's what we'll deliver each month regardless.'

commonMistakes.mistake: Publishing AI content without editing and fact-checking
commonMistakes.why: Raw AI output contains hallucinated statistics, outdated information, and detectable AI patterns. Google's Helpful Content system and manual reviewers penalize thin, AI-generated content. Clients publishing this content can see rankings drop, not rise. One viral Twitter thread calling out your client's AI content can end the relationship.
commonMistakes.prevention: Build a non-negotiable editorial process: AI drafts → human edit (especially intro, stats, examples) → fact-check all cited data → AI detection scan → publish. Budget 45-90 minutes of human editing per 1,500-word article. This is your real cost of goods.

commonMistakes.mistake: Underpricing retainers to win clients
commonMistakes.why: Operators who underprice either burn out, cut corners, or both. Underpriced clients also tend to be the most demanding.
commonMistakes.prevention: Calculate your true cost per client before pricing. Walk away from clients who won't pay it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring client reporting until they ask for it
commonMistakes.why: SEO results are invisible to clients who don't know what to look for. A client who doesn't see monthly proof of progress assumes nothing is happening and cancels. Silence between deliverables breeds doubt, even when the work is excellent.
commonMistakes.prevention: Send a short monthly report on a fixed date — even if results are early-stage. Include: keywords moving up, pages indexed, traffic trend (even if small), and what's planned next month. Use a template. 30 minutes per client per month is enough. Proactive communication is your retention strategy.

resources.whatItTakes: You're building a small agency that books sales meetings for B2B companies using cold email infrastructure, AI-powered personalization, and data enrichment tools like Clay. The actual work is less glamorous than the Twitter threads make it sound: you're pulling lead lists, writing and testing email copy, debugging deliverability issues, and reporting results to clients who are paying you to fill their calendar. The AI handles enrichment and personalization at scale — but you still have to think clearly about who the right prospect is, what they actually care about, and why your client's offer is worth a reply. If you can't answer those questions, no tool will save you. You'll need a working grasp of email infrastructure (domains, warming, SPF/DKIM), a nose for copy that doesn't sound like a robot wrote it, and enough B2B sales intuition to know a qualified lead from a time-waster. Clients will expect weekly reporting, fast responses when a campaign underperforms, and honest conversations when the numbers aren't there. This is a service business — your reputation is built one client result at a time.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most people fail at the client acquisition step before they ever get to prove their skills. They spend weeks perfecting their Clay workflows and never send a single cold email to a potential client. The second failure point is taking any client who'll pay — a mismatch between your client's offer and the market makes your campaigns look bad even when your execution is solid. Third: deliverability. Skipping proper domain warming and DNS setup tanks open rates, and new operators often don't catch it until a client is already frustrated. Finally, people underestimate how much client communication this work requires. Silent operators who only show up with a monthly report lose clients fast, even when the numbers are decent.
resources.theDip: Weeks three through eight are where this gets hard. You've got your infrastructure set up, you're running campaigns, and the results are… underwhelming. Reply rates are low, your client is asking questions you don't have great answers to, and you're second-guessing every line of copy. This is normal, and most people quit here or start chasing a different tool instead of doing the unglamorous work of testing one variable at a time. The operators who get through this dip are the ones who treat it like a diagnostic puzzle — they look at open rates vs. reply rates, they rewrite the first line, they check if the list quality is the actual problem. Results usually start clicking somewhere between weeks six and twelve, but only if you stay methodical instead of reactive.

aiPrompts.task: Diagnose a cold email campaign that isn't getting replies
aiPrompts.prompt:
I run a cold email outreach agency and one of my campaigns is underperforming. Help me diagnose the problem systematically.

Campaign stats:
- Emails sent: [NUMBER]
- Open rate: [%]
- Reply rate: [%]
- Positive reply rate: [%]
- Bounce rate: [%]
- Sequence tool used: [E.G. Instantly, Smartlead]
- Sending volume per inbox per day: [NUMBER]
- Number of sending domains/inboxes: [NUMBER]
- Days since campaign launched: [NUMBER]
- Target ICP: [DESCRIBE]
- Email 1 subject line: [PASTE IT]
- Email 1 body: [PASTE IT]

Diagnose the most likely problem by walking through this checklist:
1. Deliverability (bounce rate, spam placement, domain age, SPF/DKIM/DMARC)
2. List quality (are we hitting real people in the right role?)
3. Subject line (is it getting opens?)
4. Email body (is the opener relevant? Is the CTA too heavy?)
5. Offer clarity (would the reader immediately understand what's being offered and why it matters to them?)
6. Timing/volume (are we burning domains?)

For each issue you identify, give me: the likely cause, one specific fix I can implement this week, and what metric to watch to confirm it worked.

Be direct. Tell me the most likely culprit first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Burning new sending domains too fast
commonMistakes.why: Sending high volume from a fresh domain (less than 3-4 weeks old with no warm-up) triggers spam filters at Gmail and Outlook. Once a domain lands in spam, recovery is slow and often incomplete. Clients see zero opens, blame you, and churn.
commonMistakes.prevention: Buy domains at least 4 weeks before any campaign. Use a tool like Instantly or Smartlead's built-in warm-up for 2-3 weeks. Start at 20-30 emails/day per inbox and ramp over 2 weeks. Use aged domains from marketplaces if you need to move faster. Never share a domain across two clients.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking clients without a clear, validated ICP
commonMistakes.why: When a client says 'we sell to everyone' or can't name three specific companies they've closed, your list-building and personalization have no anchor. You'll build a generic list, write generic emails, and get generic (zero) results. You own the blame even though the offer is the problem.
commonMistakes.prevention: Before signing any client, run a 30-minute ICP interview. Require them to name: the job title who signs the check, 3 companies they've already closed, and the specific pain those companies had. If they can't answer, don't take the engagement or charge a discovery fee to define the ICP first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing activity metrics with results and reporting them to clients
commonMistakes.why: Reporting 'we sent 3,000 emails this month' as a win when zero meetings were booked destroys trust fast. Clients hired you for pipeline, not volume. Vanity metrics buy you one month; then they cancel.
commonMistakes.prevention: Set up a simple reporting dashboard (even a Google Sheet) that tracks: emails sent, open rate, reply rate, positive reply rate, and meetings booked. Report weekly. Frame every number against the goal (meetings booked). If results are below target, report it honestly with your diagnosis and next action — don't hide it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) on client domains
commonMistakes.why: Google and Microsoft now require proper authentication for bulk senders. Without it, emails go straight to spam or are rejected outright. This is a technical step most first-time operators skip because it's invisible until it's catastrophically wrong.
commonMistakes.prevention: Make domain authentication setup a mandatory step in your client onboarding checklist — before any warm-up begins. Use MXToolbox to verify SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are correctly configured. Add a DMARC policy of at least p=none with a monitoring email. Check deliverability with GlockApps or Mail-Tester before going live.

commonMistakes.mistake: Over-promising meeting volume in the sales process
commonMistakes.why: Operators desperate for clients promise '20 meetings a month' without knowing the client's offer quality, ICP clarity, or market saturation. Cold email reply rates in most B2B niches run 1-5%. The math rarely supports big meeting guarantees, and when you miss, you're liable.
commonMistakes.prevention: Quote a range based on realistic benchmarks: 'For a list of 1,000 qualified prospects, expect 10-50 replies and 3-15 positive replies in the first month, depending on offer strength and ICP fit.' Use 'meetings booked' as a lagging indicator you optimize toward, not a guarantee. Put this language in your contract.

decisionTrees.question: Should I charge a flat monthly retainer or performance-based pricing (pay-per-meeting)?

options.pickIf: You're starting out, your client's offer or ICP isn't fully validated yet, or you want predictable income.
options.nextStep: Put a 30-day cancellation clause in the contract.

options.pickIf: This model has higher upside but higher risk.
options.nextStep: Define 'qualified meeting' precisely in the contract (attended call, right job title, right company size). Set a monthly minimum to cover your costs. This model works best as an upsell for existing retainer clients once you've proven results.

options.pickIf: Client is skeptical of retainer-only and wants skin in the game from you, but you also need cost coverage.
options.nextStep: Cap the bonus at a reasonable ceiling so a great month doesn't create billing surprises for the client. Track meetings in a shared doc the client can see in real time.

decisionTrees.question: A potential client wants results in 2 weeks. How do you handle it?

options.choice: Set honest expectations and take the client
options.pickIf: They understand that week 1-2 is setup and warm-up, and they're measuring success at the 30-60 day mark. Get this in writing.
options.nextStep: Use aged domains (buy from a domain marketplace) to skip the 2-3 week cold warm-up period. Start warm-up immediately on day 1. Begin list building and copy in parallel so you're ready to send the moment domains are warm.

options.choice: Push back and reset the timeline
options.pickIf: They're expecting meetings booked in 14 days and won't budge. This is a red flag client — they don't understand the channel and will blame you for the infrastructure reality.
options.nextStep: Explain the warm-up requirement plainly. If they still push, decline the engagement or charge a premium rush fee that covers the risk of using shortcuts (higher volume, faster ramp) that may hurt deliverability.

options.pickIf: They've already had a bad experience with another agency, expect guarantees, and are hostile about the timeline. The energy cost of managing an unrealistic client will tank your other accounts.
options.nextStep: Refer them to someone else or suggest they try LinkedIn outreach (faster to start) while you set up email infrastructure properly. Protect your bandwidth for clients who will become case studies.

decisionTrees.question: You've maxed out at 4-5 clients solo. Should you hire or cap growth?

options.choice: Hire a part-time VA for list building and reporting
options.pickIf: You're spending more than 8 hours/week on Clay workflows, list cleaning, and weekly report formatting — tasks that don't require your strategic judgment.
options.nextStep: Build SOPs in Loom videos before handing off. This frees you to take 2-3 more clients.

options.pickIf: You don't want management overhead and your current clients are sticky.
options.nextStep: Focus on one niche (e.g., only SaaS, only logistics) so your playbooks compound and your results get better with each client.

options.choice: Build a productized service and add an account manager
options.pickIf: This shifts you from operator to agency owner.
options.nextStep: Hire a part-time account manager to own client communication and reporting. You own strategy and new client sales. Standardize everything into SOPs. Budget 3-6 months for the transition to feel smooth.

aiPrompts.task: Comparison content (Tool A vs B for [niche])
aiPrompts.prompt:
Write an honest comparison post: [Tool A] vs [Tool B] for [niche persona].

My affiliate: [Tool A or B — be transparent about which]
My honest take: [where each one wins]

Structure:

INTRO (200 words):
- Who this comparison is for
- TL;DR verdict (one-line)
- Honest disclosure ("I'm an affiliate for X but I'll tell you when Y is better")

COMPARISON SECTIONS (5-7):
- Pricing
- Core features
- Niche-specific use case
- Onboarding ease
- Customer support
- Ecosystem / integrations
- Long-term scalability

In each section: bullet who wins + why.

VERDICT:
- "Pick A if [criteria]"
- "Pick B if [criteria]"
- "Use both if [advanced case]"

DISCLOSURE FOOTER:
- FTC-compliant affiliate disclosure
- Note: comparison content converts 2-3x better than reviews because buyers searching "X vs Y" are deep in research mode.

commonMistakes.mistake: Promoting too early (before audience trust)
commonMistakes.why: Audiences detect affiliate pitches. Pitching before establishing authority = unsubscribes + reputation damage.
commonMistakes.prevention: Build for 3-6 months before first pitch. Welcome sequence soft-introduces. Hard pitch only at email 12+.

commonMistakes.mistake: Promoting products you have not used
commonMistakes.why: Buyers ask specific questions. Generic answers reveal you have not used the product. Trust collapses.
commonMistakes.prevention: Use every product you promote. Document your real workflow. Make case studies from your usage.

commonMistakes.mistake: No email list
commonMistakes.why: Algorithms own social. Email is the only owned channel. Without it, every sale is a one-off.
commonMistakes.prevention: Email list from day 1. Lead magnet → ConvertKit/Beehiiv. Email outperforms social for high-ticket.

commonMistakes.mistake: Going broad ("marketing tips") vs niche-specific
commonMistakes.why: Niche audiences do.
commonMistakes.prevention: Pick a specific persona × specific outcome. "AI tools for solo lawyers" beats "AI tips."

commonMistakes.mistake: Missing recurring B2B SaaS commissions
commonMistakes.why: Most affiliates only count one-time payouts. Recurring SaaS commissions compound dramatically.

commonMistakes.mistake: No partner relationships
commonMistakes.why: Solo growth is slow. Cross-newsletter swaps + co-promotions compound.
commonMistakes.prevention: Reach out to 5-10 niche creators monthly. Propose value-first swaps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Affiliate disclosure violations
commonMistakes.why: FTC enforces affiliate disclosures. Hidden affiliate links = fines + program termination.
commonMistakes.prevention: Visible disclosure on every affiliate piece. "I may earn a commission..." in posts + emails + videos.
